A: Chapter 4 moves in six steps. (1) 4.1–3: the Lord declares that he taught this imperishable yoga to Vivasvat, who passed it to Manu and Ikṣvāku; known by the royal sages through succession, it was lost over time, and he now teaches it again to Arjuna as his devotee and friend. (2) 4.4–10: to Arjuna's question how he could have taught it before Vivasvat, the Lord answers that he knows his many births; unborn and lord of beings, he comes into being by his own māyā whenever dharma declines, to protect the good, destroy wrongdoers and establish dharma; whoever knows his divine birth and action is not reborn and comes to him, as many have, purified by knowledge. (3) 4.11–15: he receives people as they approach him; result-seekers worship the gods; he made the four classes by guṇa and action yet is a non-doer, unstained by action; knowing this, the ancients acted, so Arjuna should act. (4) 4.16–23: what action, wrong action and inaction are; the wise see inaction in action; the one free of desire, whose actions are burnt in the fire of knowledge, is not bound though acting. (5) 4.24–32: action as sacrifice — Brahman is every element of the offering — and a list of the many kinds of sacrifice (to the gods, of the senses, of breath, of things, of austerity, of study and knowledge), all born of action. (6) 4.33–42: the sacrifice of knowledge is best, all action culminating in knowledge; knowledge is to be learned from seers of truth by prostration, questioning and service; it is a raft over all wrong, a fire burning all action, the supreme purifier, won by the faithful and self-restrained and bringing peace, while the doubter perishes; the chapter ends: cut doubt with the sword of knowledge, resort to yoga and stand up. Purpose, as the chapter presents it: to establish the ancient authority of the teaching and the Lord who gives it, and to show that action done as sacrifice, without attachment, culminates in knowledge, so that Arjuna may act free of doubt.
B: Chapter 4 (Kṛṣṇa to Arjuna, with one question from Arjuna) moves as follows. (1) 4.1–3: the imperishable yoga was taught by Kṛṣṇa to Vivasvat, passed to Manu and Ikṣvāku and known by the royal sages through succession, was lost over time, and is now re-told to Arjuna as devotee and friend. (2) 4.4–10: Arjuna asks how Kṛṣṇa could have taught Vivasvat; Kṛṣṇa answers that he and Arjuna have had many births which he alone knows; though unborn and lord of beings he comes into being by his own māyā whenever dharma declines, to protect the good and establish dharma; knowing his divine birth and action frees one from rebirth, and many purified by knowledge have reached his state. (3) 4.11–15: he responds to people as they approach him; people sacrifice to deities for quick success; he made the fourfold class-order yet is a non-doer, unstained by action, and the ancients seeking liberation acted knowing this — so Arjuna should act. (4) 4.16–23: the difficult analysis of action, wrong action (vikarma) and inaction; the wise one sees inaction in action, acts without desire or attachment to fruit, his actions burnt by the fire of knowledge, and is not bound. (5) 4.24–32: sacrifice (yajña) extended: every factor of the offering is Brahman, and a catalogue of sacrifices (to the gods, into Brahman, senses into restraint, objects into senses, breath, material goods, austerity, yoga, recitation and knowledge, breath-regulation, regulated food), all born of action. (6) 4.33–42: the sacrifice of knowledge is superior and all action culminates in knowledge; knowledge is to be learnt from truth-seeing knowers by prostration, questioning and service; it is a raft, a fire, the supreme purifier, gained by faith and sense-control and leading to peace; the doubter perishes; Arjuna is to cut his doubt with the sword of knowledge, resort to yoga and stand up. Purpose, as the chapter presents it: to ground the teaching of action in an ancient divine transmission and in the Lord's own nature, and to show action performed with knowledge, as sacrifice, as not binding.

A: Chapter 5 moves in five steps. (1) 5.1–6: Arjuna asks which is better, the renunciation of actions or yoga; the Lord answers that both lead to the highest good but the yoga of action is superior; the constant renunciant is the one without aversion or desire; only the childish call Sāṃkhya and Yoga separate, since both reach the same place; renunciation is hard without yoga. (2) 5.7–12: the one yoked in yoga is not stained though acting; the knower of reality thinks 'I do nothing', holding that the senses move among their objects; acting with actions placed in Brahman and without attachment, one is unstained like a lotus leaf; yogins act for self-purification; abandoning the fruit brings peace, attachment to it binds. (3) 5.13–17: the embodied one, having renounced all actions mentally, sits in the city of nine gates neither acting nor causing action; the master creates neither agency nor actions nor their fruit — nature acts; knowledge is covered by ignorance, and when ignorance is destroyed knowledge shines like the sun and those intent on That reach non-return. (4) 5.18–26: the wise see the same in all beings; those established in sameness are established in Brahman, which is flawless and the same; unmoved by pleasant and unpleasant, finding happiness within rather than in contact-born pleasures, withstanding desire and anger, having happiness, delight and light within, the yogin becomes Brahman and attains brahma-nirvāṇa, which surrounds the self-knowing ascetics. (5) 5.27–29: an outline of meditation (external contacts put outside, gaze between the brows, prāṇa and apāna made equal) for the sage intent on liberation, who is ever free; and the closing: knowing the Lord as enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, great lord of all worlds and friend of all beings, one attains peace. Purpose, as the chapter presents it: to answer the question of renunciation versus action by showing that true renunciation is inner and that yoga leads to the same goal, the peace of brahma-nirvāṇa.
B: Chapter 5 (Kṛṣṇa to Arjuna, opened by Arjuna's question) moves as follows. (1) 5.1: Arjuna asks which is better, renunciation of actions (saṃnyāsa) or yoga. (2) 5.2–6: both lead to the highest good, but the yoga of action is superior; the constant renouncer is one who neither hates nor craves; only the childish separate Sāṃkhya and Yoga, which reach the same place; renunciation is hard to attain without yoga. (3) 5.7–12: the one yoked in yoga, whose self has become the self of all beings, acts without being stained; the knower thinks 'I do nothing', the senses move among their objects; placing actions in Brahman and giving up attachment he is untouched like a lotus leaf; yogins act for self-purification; giving up the fruit brings lasting peace, while desire binds. (4) 5.13–17: the embodied one, having renounced actions mentally, dwells in the nine-gated city neither acting nor causing action; the lord does not create agency or its fruits — svabhāva acts; knowledge is covered by ignorance, and when ignorance is destroyed knowledge lights up the highest; those devoted to That go to non-return. (5) 5.18–26: the learned see all beings equally; those established in sameness conquer the world here, for Brahman is the same; the knower of Brahman is unmoved by pleasant and unpleasant, finds happiness within; contact-born pleasures are wombs of sorrow; withstanding desire and anger, with inner happiness, delight and light, the yogin becomes Brahman and attains brahma-nirvāṇa. (6) 5.27–28: a brief instruction (external contacts shut out, gaze between the brows, prāṇa and apāna made even) describing the sage who is forever free. (7) 5.29: knowing Kṛṣṇa as enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, great lord of all worlds and friend of all beings, one attains peace. Purpose, as the chapter presents it: to answer the question of renunciation versus the yoga of action by showing that true renunciation is inward and that disciplined action leads to the same goal, brahma-nirvāṇa and peace.
resolution: merged: Chapter 5 moves in seven steps. (1) 5.1: Arjuna asks which is better, the renunciation of actions (saṃnyāsa) or yoga, since Kṛṣṇa praises both. (2) 5.2–6: both lead to the highest good, but the yoga of action is superior to the renunciation of action; the constant renouncer is the one who neither hates nor desires; only the childish, not the learned, call Sāṃkhya and Yoga separate, since the same place is reached by both; renunciation is hard to attain without yoga, while the sage yoked in yoga soon reaches Brahman. (3) 5.7–12: the one yoked in yoga, whose self has become the self of all beings, is not stained though acting; the yoked knower of reality thinks 'I do nothing', holding that the senses move among their objects; one who acts placing actions in Brahman and abandoning attachment is unstained, like a lotus leaf by water; yogins act for the purification of the self; the yoked one who gives up the fruit attains lasting peace, while the unyoked, attached to the fruit through desire, is bound. (4) 5.13–17: the embodied one, having renounced all actions with the mind, dwells at ease in the city of nine gates, neither acting nor causing action; the master (prabhu) creates neither agency nor actions nor their link with the fruit — inherent nature (svabhāva) acts; knowledge is covered by ignorance and so creatures are deluded, but where ignorance is destroyed by knowledge, knowledge illumines the highest like the sun, and those intent on That go to non-return. (5) 5.18–26: the learned see the same in all beings; those whose mind rests in sameness conquer creation here and are established in Brahman, which is flawless and the same; the knower of Brahman is unmoved by the pleasant and the unpleasant; unattached to external contacts he finds the happiness that is in the self, for contact-born enjoyments are wombs of sorrow; one who withstands the surge of desire and anger is yoked and happy; the yogin with happiness, delight and light within, having become Brahman, attains brahma-nirvāṇa, which lies near the self-knowing ascetics free of desire and anger. (6) 5.27–28: in outline, a practice (external contacts put outside, the gaze between the brows, prāṇa and apāna made even) of the sage intent on liberation, who is ever free. (7) 5.29: knowing the Lord as enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, great lord of all the worlds and friend of all beings, one attains peace. Purpose, as the chapter presents it: to answer the question of renunciation versus the yoga of action by showing that true renunciation is inward, that the two reach the same goal, and that the goal is brahma-nirvāṇa and peace.

A: Chapter 6 moves in eight steps. (1) 6.1–4: the one who does the required action without depending on its fruit is both renunciant and yogin; renunciation is yoga, for no one is a yogin without renouncing intention; for one ascending to yoga action is the means, for one who has ascended calm is the means. (2) 6.5–9: one should raise the self by the self, which is its own friend or enemy; the conquered, calm self is composed amid the opposites; the yoked yogin sees clod, stone and gold alike and regards friend and foe, good and wicked with an equal mind. (3) 6.10–17: the practice of meditation — solitude, a clean place and a firm seat, one-pointed mind, body, head and neck in line, gaze at the nose-tip, fearlessness, the vow of the brahmacārin, the mind on the Lord — bringing peace that culminates in nirvāṇa; and moderation in food, recreation, effort, sleep and waking. (4) 6.18–28: the yoked mind is like a lamp in a windless place; the state where the stilled mind rests and the self sees the self, knowing boundless happiness beyond the senses and unshaken by sorrow, is called yoga, the disconnection from union with suffering; the method of gradually stilling the mind and bringing it back whenever it wanders; the calmed yogin attains the highest happiness, contact with Brahman. (5) 6.29–32: the yoked one sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self; whoever sees the Lord everywhere is never lost to him; the highest yogin sees pleasure and pain everywhere by likeness to himself. (6) 6.33–36: Arjuna objects that the mind is too restless for such sameness; the Lord grants this but says it is held by practice and dispassion, and yoga is attainable by the self-controlled through right means. (7) 6.37–45: Arjuna asks the fate of the faithful one who falls from yoga; the Lord answers that no doer of good is lost: he dwells in the worlds of the meritorious, is reborn among the pure and prosperous or among yogins, regains his former understanding, is carried by former practice, and, perfected over many births, reaches the highest goal. (8) 6.46–47: the yogin surpasses ascetics, knowers and ritualists, so Arjuna should be a yogin; of all yogins the one who worships the Lord with faith, his inner self gone into him, is the most yoked. Purpose, as the chapter presents it: to set out the discipline of meditation and its fruit, to reassure the practitioner about restlessness and failure, and to place devotion to the Lord at the summit of yoga.
B: Chapter 6 (Kṛṣṇa to Arjuna, with Arjuna's two questions) moves as follows. (2) 6.5–9: one must raise oneself by oneself — the self is its own friend or enemy; the self-conquered, tranquil yogin is steady in all pairs of opposites, satisfied with knowledge, and equal toward all. (3) 6.10–17: instruction in meditation — solitude, a clean firm seat, one-pointed mind, erect posture, gaze toward the nose-tip, celibacy, mind fixed on Kṛṣṇa — leading to peace culminating in nirvāṇa; moderation in food, recreation, sleep and waking. (4) 6.18–23: the state of yoga: the controlled mind resting in the self like a lamp in a windless place; the mind stilled, the self seen by the self, boundless happiness beyond the senses, unshaken by sorrow — this is yoga, the unyoking from union with sorrow, to be practised with resolve. (5) 6.24–28: method: giving up desires born of intention, gradually coming to rest with a firm intellect, thinking of nothing, bringing back the wandering mind; the result is supreme happiness, becoming Brahman, contact with Brahman. (6) 6.29–32: the yogin sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self, sees Kṛṣṇa everywhere, worships him in all beings established in oneness, and regards others' pleasure and pain as his own. (7) 6.33–36: Arjuna objects that the mind is too restless; Kṛṣṇa grants it but says it is held by practice (abhyāsa) and dispassion (vairāgya). (8) 6.37–45: Arjuna asks the fate of one who has faith but falls from yoga; Kṛṣṇa answers that no doer of good perishes — he dwells in meritorious worlds, is reborn among the pure or among yogins, regains his former understanding, is carried by former practice, and, perfected through many births, reaches the highest goal. (9) 6.46–47: the yogin is greater than ascetics, knowers and ritualists — be a yogin; and among yogins the one who worships Kṛṣṇa with faith and inner self fixed on him is the most yoked. Purpose, as the chapter presents it: to set out the discipline of meditative yoga (its prerequisites, method, state and result), to reassure about failure in it, and to crown it with faith-filled worship of the Lord.
resolution: merged: Chapter 6 moves in nine steps. (1) 6.1–4: the one who does the action that is to be done without depending on its fruit is both renouncer and yogin, not one who merely gives up the sacred fires and rites; what is called renunciation is yoga, for no one becomes a yogin without renouncing intention (saṅkalpa); for the sage wishing to ascend to yoga action is the means, for the one who has ascended calm (śama) is the means, and he has ascended when he is attached neither to sense-objects nor to actions. (2) 6.5–9: one should raise the self by the self, which is its own friend or enemy; for the self-conquered and tranquil the supreme self is composed amid the pairs of opposites; the yoked yogin, satisfied with knowledge and realized knowledge, sees clod, stone and gold alike and has an equal mind toward friend and foe, the good and the wicked. (3) 6.10–17: instruction in meditation — solitude, a firm seat in a clean place, the mind made one-pointed, body, head and neck held in line, the gaze toward the nose-tip, fearlessness, the vow of the brahmacārin, the mind fixed on and intent on the Lord — leading to the peace that culminates in nirvāṇa; yoga is for one measured in food, recreation, effort, sleep and waking. (4) 6.18–23: the state of yoga: the restrained mind resting in the self alone, steady like a lamp in a windless place; the mind stilled, the self seen by the self, boundless happiness beyond the senses, no gain counted higher, not shaken even by heavy sorrow — this is to be known as yoga, the unyoking from union with sorrow, to be practised with resolve and an undejected mind. (5) 6.24–28: the method: abandoning desires born of intention and restraining the senses, coming to rest little by little with an intellect held firm, making the mind abide in the self and thinking of nothing, bringing the restless mind back whenever it wanders; the result: supreme happiness, becoming Brahman, the boundless happiness of contact with Brahman. (6) 6.29–32: the yoked one sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self; whoever sees the Lord everywhere and everything in him is not lost to him; the yogin established in oneness who worships him as abiding in all beings abides in him however he lives; the highest yogin sees pleasure and pain everywhere by likeness to himself. (9) 6.46–47: the yogin is greater than ascetics, knowers and performers of works, so Arjuna should be a yogin; and of all yogins the one who worships the Lord with faith, his inner self gone into him, is the most yoked. Purpose, as the chapter presents it: to set out the discipline of meditative yoga — its prerequisites, method, state and result — to reassure the practitioner about restlessness and failure, and to place faithful worship of the Lord at the summit of yoga.
